s.u1.title: The atom comes apart
s.u1.blurb: Dalton said the atom could not be divided. Three particles later, it can.
s.u2.title: Three models, each fixing the last
s.u2.blurb: Every model here was proposed because the one before it failed at something specific.
s.u3.title: Where the electrons sit
s.u3.blurb: Not anywhere. Shells, in a fixed order, with a fixed capacity.
s.u4.title: Valency, explained at last
s.u4.blurb: The arms you were asked to take on trust in the last chapter turn out to be electrons.
s.u5.title: Counting what is inside
s.u5.blurb: Two numbers tell you everything about what is in a nucleus.
s.u6.title: Same element, different weight
s.u6.blurb: Why chlorine weighs 35.5 when no chlorine atom does.
ch4.u1.comb.predict.prompt: You run a dry comb through your hair, then hold it over small pieces of paper. What happens?
ch4.u1.comb.predict.o0: Nothing, a comb is not a magnet
ch4.u1.comb.predict.o2: The paper jumps up to the comb
ch4.u1.comb.predict.o3: Only metal combs would do anything
ch4.u1.comb.observe: The comb was not charged before you rubbed it. Where did the charge come from?
ch4.u1.comb.explain: Rubbing moved something between the hair and the comb. Whatever moved carries charge, and it came out of ordinary matter, which means ordinary matter has charged pieces inside it.
ch4.u1.do.steps:
1. Tear paper into pieces smaller than a grain of rice.
2. Run the comb through dry hair ten or twelve times.
3. Hold the comb just above the paper and watch.
4. Now rub the glass rod with the silk cloth.
5. Bring the rod near the inflated balloon and watch what the balloon does.
ch4.u1.do.watch: It fails on a humid day, and that is worth knowing rather than hiding. Damp air carries the charge away as fast as rubbing puts it there. If nothing happens, dry the comb and the hair and try again.
ask.ch4-u1-do-1.wherefrom.q: If the comb ends up charged, does the hair end up charged too?
ask.ch4-u1-do-1.wherefrom.a:
Yes, and oppositely. Nothing was created by the rubbing: electrons were moved from one surface to the other. The comb gains them and becomes negative, the hair loses them and is left positive.

That is why the experiment is evidence for anything at all. If rubbing made charge out of nothing, it would tell you nothing about what matter is made of. Because it only moves charge, the charge had to be sitting inside both of them beforehand.
a.ch4-u1-do-1.title: Rub a comb and pick up paper
a.ch4-u1-do-1.blurb: Two ways to charge something by rubbing it. Both work, and neither needs anything you cannot find at home.
ch4.u1.definition: An atom is not the smallest thing there is. J. J. Thomson found the electron, which carries a negative charge and almost no mass. E. Goldstein found positive rays in a discharge tube, which led to the proton: one unit of positive charge, and about 2000 times the mass of an electron. J. Chadwick found the neutron in 1932: the same mass as a proton, and no charge at all. An atom is these three, and nothing else.
a.ch4-u1-read-2.title: Three particles, and who found them
ch4.u1.sort.i0.label: Negative charge
ch4.u1.sort.i0.why: The only negative one of the three.
ch4.u1.sort.i1.label: Mass so small it is treated as nothing
ch4.u1.sort.i1.why: About one two-thousandth of a proton, so it is left out of mass sums.
ch4.u1.sort.i2.label: Found outside the nucleus
ch4.u1.sort.i2.why: The only one of the three that is not a nucleon.
ch4.u1.sort.i3.label: Positive charge, one unit
ch4.u1.sort.i3.why: Equal and opposite to the electron's.
ch4.u1.sort.i4.label: Its count decides which element you have
ch4.u1.sort.i4.why: Change it and you have changed the element. Nothing else does that.
ch4.u1.sort.i5.label: No charge at all
ch4.u1.sort.i5.why: Which is why it went undiscovered until 1932, long after the other two.
ch4.u1.sort.i6.label: Same mass as a proton
ch4.u1.sort.i6.why: Nearly. Both are taken as one unit.
ch4.u1.sort.i7.label: Absent from ordinary hydrogen
ch4.u1.sort.i7.why: Hydrogen's usual atom is one proton and one electron, and nothing else.
ask.ch4-u1-sort-3.neutronlate.q: Why was the neutron found so much later than the other two?
ask.ch4-u1-sort-3.neutronlate.a:
Because every method they had for finding particles worked by watching charge, and the neutron has none.

An electron can be pulled by a magnet and bent off course. A proton can too, the other way. A neutron sails through both untouched, leaves no track, and triggers nothing that detects charge. Chadwick had to find it indirectly, by firing radiation at beryllium and showing that whatever came out knocked protons loose while being bent by no field at all.

It is a good example of a general problem: an instrument finds the things it was built to notice.
a.ch4-u1-sort-3.title: Which particle does this describe?
a.ch4-u1-sort-3.blurb: Charge, mass and where it sits. Each description belongs to exactly one of the three.
ch4.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: Which particle has a mass of about one two-thousandth of the others?
ch4.u1.quiz.q0.f0: A proton is one of the heavy two.
ch4.u1.quiz.q0.f1: A neutron is the other heavy one.
ch4.u1.quiz.q0.f2: Right. It is so light that mass sums ignore it entirely.
ch4.u1.quiz.q0.o3: They all have the same mass
ch4.u1.quiz.q0.f3: Two of them are about equal. The third is nothing like either.
ch4.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: An atom has no overall charge. Why?
ch4.u1.quiz.q1.f0: It contains two kinds of charged particle, in quantity.
ch4.u1.quiz.q1.o1: The neutrons cancel out the charges
ch4.u1.quiz.q1.f1: Neutrons have no charge, so they cannot cancel anything.
ch4.u1.quiz.q1.o2: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons
ch4.u1.quiz.q1.f2: Right. Equal and opposite, so the total is nothing.
ch4.u1.quiz.q1.o3: The charges leak away into the air
ch4.u1.quiz.q1.f3: Nothing leaks. The balance is built in.
a.ch4-u1-quiz-4.title: The three particles
ch4.u2.thomson: Thomson's atom was a ball of positive charge with electrons stuck in it, like dry fruit in a Christmas pudding or seeds in a watermelon. It had one real virtue: it explained why an atom is electrically neutral, with the positive and negative in equal measure. What it could not survive was being tested.
a.ch4-u2-read-1.title: Thomson: charge spread through a pudding
ch4.u2.foil.predict.prompt: If Thomson were right and charge is spread evenly through every atom, what should fast alpha particles do when fired at gold foil?
ch4.u2.foil.predict.o0: Nearly all pass straight through, a few bounce right back
ch4.u2.foil.predict.o1: All of them pass through with at most a slight nudge
ch4.u2.foil.predict.o3: They stop dead inside the foil
ch4.u2.foil.observe: One alpha particle in twelve thousand came back. What has to be true for that to happen?
ch4.u2.foil.explain: Thomson's atom predicts gentle nudges and nothing more, because a thinly spread charge has nowhere concentrated enough to turn a fast heavy particle around. Rebounds mean the positive charge is packed into something tiny and dense, which is the nucleus.
ch4.u2.rutherford: Most alpha particles went straight through, so most of the atom is empty. A few bent by small angles, so something positive is in there. About one in twelve thousand came back the way it came, which Rutherford said was as incredible as a shell bouncing off tissue paper. All the positive charge, and nearly all the mass, sits in a nucleus about a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom around it.
ask.ch4-u2-read-2.whygold.q: Why gold? Would any metal have done?
ask.ch4-u2-read-2.whygold.a:
Gold because it can be beaten thinner than anything else, and thinness is the whole experiment.

A thick foil would deflect each particle several times over, and a particle that came back might have been turned by a dozen glancing blows rather than one violent encounter. At about a thousand atoms thick you can argue that a rebound was a single event, and only then does it tell you something is small, hard and massive in there.

Another metal would give the same result, with a weaker argument.
a.ch4-u2-read-2.title: Rutherford fires at gold foil
a.ch4-u2-read-2.blurb: A sheet of gold about a thousand atoms thick, and fast alpha particles aimed straight at it.
ch4.u2.sort.i0.label: Positive charge spread through the whole atom
ch4.u2.sort.i1.label: Electrons embedded like seeds in a watermelon
ch4.u2.sort.i2.label: Nearly all the mass in a tiny central nucleus
ch4.u2.sort.i2.why: What the rebounds forced him to.
ch4.u2.sort.i3.label: Electrons moving in circular paths around the centre
ch4.u2.sort.i3.why: Which is also where its trouble starts.
ch4.u2.sort.i4.label: Most of the atom is empty space
ch4.u2.sort.i4.why: Most alpha particles met nothing at all.
ch4.u2.sort.i5.label: Electrons allowed only in certain fixed orbits
ch4.u2.sort.i5.why: The move that rescued the atom from collapsing.
ch4.u2.sort.i6.label: An electron in its orbit radiates no energy
ch4.u2.sort.i6.why: Asserted, because the alternative is an atom that does not last.
ask.ch4-u2-sort-3.collapse.a:
Because a charge going round a circle is accelerating, even at a steady speed, since its direction keeps changing. Accelerating charges radiate energy. An electron losing energy spirals inward, and the sum says it would reach the nucleus almost instantly.

So Rutherford's atom should last a fraction of a second, and atoms have lasted for billions of years. Bohr's answer was not to explain the contradiction away but to rule it out: electrons may occupy only certain orbits, and in those they simply do not radiate. It was an assertion that worked, and the reason why took another decade.
a.ch4-u2-sort-3.title: Which model claimed this?
a.ch4-u2-sort-3.blurb: Three models in order. Each one keeps what worked and fixes what did not.
ch4.u2.quiz.q0.prompt: Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment was responsible for discovering what?
ch4.u2.quiz.q0.f0: Thomson found the electron, and earlier.
ch4.u2.quiz.q0.f1: Right. The rebounds are what put a nucleus in the picture.
ch4.u2.quiz.q0.f2: The proton came from Goldstein's work on canal rays.
ch4.u2.quiz.q1.prompt: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What does that tell you?
ch4.u2.quiz.q1.o0: The foil had holes in it
ch4.u2.quiz.q1.f0: It was continuous foil. The gaps are inside the atoms, not between them.
ch4.u2.quiz.q1.o1: Most of an atom is empty space
ch4.u2.quiz.q1.f1: Right. There was simply nothing in the way for most of them.
ch4.u2.quiz.q1.f2: Their size is not the point. They went through because there was nothing to hit.
ch4.u2.quiz.q1.f3: Softness is not a property atoms have.
a.ch4-u2-quiz-4.title: What each experiment showed
ch4.u3.definition: Electrons sit in shells, counted outwards from the nucleus and named K, L, M, N. The most a shell can hold is 2n squared, where n is its number: 2 in K, 8 in L, 18 in M, 32 in N. Two rules go with it. The outermost shell never holds more than 8, and a shell does not start filling until the ones inside it are full.
a.ch4-u3-read-1.title: Shells, and how many fit in each
ch4.bohr.nucleus.label: The nucleus
ch4.bohr.nucleus.do: Draw a small filled circle right in the middle. Leave plenty of room around it.
ch4.bohr.nucleus.does: Eleven protons and twelve neutrons, packed into a space about a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom you are drawing. Nearly all the mass of the atom is in this dot.
ch4.bohr.nucleus.detail.p0: Sodium has 11 protons, so its atomic number is 11.
ch4.bohr.nucleus.detail.p1: It has 12 neutrons, so its mass number is 11 plus 12, which is 23.
ch4.bohr.nucleus.detail.p2: Drawn to scale the nucleus would be invisible here. Every Bohr diagram cheats on this.
ch4.bohr.kshell.label: The K shell
ch4.bohr.kshell.do: Draw a circle around the nucleus, about a finger's width out.
ch4.bohr.kshell.does: The first shell, n equals 1. Its capacity is 2 times 1 squared, which is 2.
ch4.bohr.ke.label: Two electrons in K
ch4.bohr.ke.do: Put two dots on that circle, opposite each other.
ch4.bohr.ke.does: K is now full. Nothing else can go in, and nothing starts filling L until this is done.
ch4.bohr.lshell.label: The L shell
ch4.bohr.lshell.do: Draw a second circle outside the first, about the same gap again.
ch4.bohr.lshell.does: The second shell, n equals 2. Capacity 2 times 2 squared, which is 8.
ch4.bohr.le.label: Eight electrons in L
ch4.bohr.le.do: Space eight dots evenly around the second circle.
ch4.bohr.le.does: L is full too. Sodium has used 10 of its 11 electrons and has one left.
ch4.bohr.mshell.label: The M shell
ch4.bohr.mshell.do: Draw a third circle outside the second.
ch4.bohr.mshell.does: The third shell, n equals 3. It could hold 18, but it will not need to here.
ch4.bohr.me.label: The last electron
ch4.bohr.me.do: Put a single dot on the outer circle.
ch4.bohr.me.does: This lone electron is sodium's entire chemistry. It is loosely held, easily lost, and it is why sodium has a valency of one.
ch4.bohr.me.detail.p0: The electron distribution of sodium is written 2,8,1.
ch4.bohr.me.detail.p1: One electron in the outermost shell means one electron to lose, so valency 1.
ch4.bohr.me.detail.p2: Lose it and you have Na+, which has the full shells of neon and is far happier.
ch4.bohr.me.detail.p3: This is the arm that Chapter 3 drew on magnesium and sodium without explaining.
ch4.bohr.caption: A sodium atom, 2,8,1
ask.ch4-u3-draw-2.notorbits.q: Are the electrons really going round in circles like that?
ask.ch4-u3-draw-2.notorbits.a:
No, and the diagram is a bookkeeping device rather than a picture.

What survives from it is true and useful: electrons occupy shells, the shells have capacities, and the outermost one decides the chemistry. What is not true is the neat circular path. An electron does not have a position and a speed in the way a planet does, and a later model replaced the orbit with a cloud of probability.

It is worth knowing you are being told a simplification, because this one gets replaced in a couple of years and students who were never warned feel cheated.
a.ch4-u3-draw-2.title: Build a sodium atom, shell by shell
a.ch4-u3-draw-2.blurb: Seven steps, drawn in the order the shells actually fill. Copy each one as it appears, and tap any part to ask what it does.
ch4.u3.calc.c0.prompt: The capacity of a shell is 2n squared, where n is the shell number. How many electrons fit in the M shell, which is the third?
ch4.u3.calc.c0.g1: M is the third shell, so n is 3
ch4.u3.calc.c0.s0: Square the shell number: 3 squared is 9
ch4.u3.calc.c0.trap: Answering 8. That is the limit on an outermost shell, not the capacity of M.
ch4.u3.calc.c1.prompt: Potassium has 19 electrons. K holds 2 and L holds 8. M can hold 18, but no outermost shell may hold more than 8. How many electrons end up in the outermost shell of potassium?
ch4.u3.calc.c1.g2: M takes 8, because it would be outermost with 9
ch4.u3.calc.c1.s0: Fill K and L: that is 10
ch4.u3.calc.c1.s1: M takes 8, which brings the total to 18
ch4.u3.calc.c1.s2: One electron is left, and it starts the N shell
ch4.u3.calc.c1.trap: Putting 9 in M. The outermost shell rule caps it at 8, which is exactly why potassium starts a fourth shell with one electron and behaves like sodium.
a.ch4-u3-calc-3.title: How many fit?
ch4.u3.quiz.q0.prompt: Which of these is the correct electron distribution for sodium?
ch4.u3.quiz.q0.f0: Shells fill from the inside out, and K only holds 2.
ch4.u3.quiz.q0.f1: L has to be full before M starts.
ch4.u3.quiz.q0.f2: Right. K takes 2, L takes 8, and the last one goes to M.
ch4.u3.quiz.q0.f3: That fills the shells in the wrong order entirely.
ch4.u3.quiz.q1.prompt: If the K and L shells of an atom are full, how many electrons does it have?
ch4.u3.quiz.q1.f1: Right. 2 in K and 8 in L makes 10, which is neon.
ch4.u3.quiz.q1.f2: That would need M filled too.
a.ch4-u3-quiz-4.title: Filling the shells
ch4.u4.definition: The electrons in the outermost shell are the valence electrons, and they are the only ones that take part in chemistry. A full outer shell of eight, an octet, is stable and unreactive, which is why the noble gases do nothing. Every other atom reaches for that octet by losing, gaining or sharing electrons. The number it has to move is its valency, which is where Chapter 3's arms came from.
a.ch4-u4-read-1.title: The arms were electrons all along
ch4.u4.why.predict.prompt: Magnesium's shells are 2,8,2. Why does it have a valency of two?
ch4.u4.why.predict.o1: Because it has two electrons in its outermost shell
ch4.u4.why.predict.o2: Because it is the second element in its group
ch4.u4.why.predict.o3: Because its mass number is even
ch4.u4.why.observe: Count the outermost electrons of each atom as you join them up.
ch4.u4.why.explain: Two electrons in the outer shell, two electrons to lose, two arms. Chlorine has seven and needs one more, so one arm. The crossing-over trick from last chapter was a shadow of this.
ask.ch4-u4-valencyhands-2.fluorine.q: Fluorine has seven outer electrons. Why is its valency one and not seven?
ask.ch4-u4-valencyhands-2.fluorine.a:
Because it takes the cheaper route. Fluorine could in principle lose all seven to empty its outer shell, or gain one to fill it. Gaining one is enormously easier than tearing seven away, so that is what happens, and the valency is one.

The general rule is that an atom does whichever is the shorter journey to a full shell. Up to four outer electrons it tends to lose them; above four it gains the few it is missing. That is why valency rises from 1 to 4 across the first half of a period and then falls back down to 0.
a.ch4-u4-valencyhands-2.title: The same arms, now with a reason
a.ch4-u4-valencyhands-2.blurb: The same puzzle as the last chapter, except now you can say where each arm comes from.
ch4.u4.sort.i0.label: Sodium, 2,8,1
ch4.u4.sort.i0.why: One electron out and the full L shell is exposed.
ch4.u4.sort.i1.label: Magnesium, 2,8,2
ch4.u4.sort.i2.label: Aluminium, 2,8,3
ch4.u4.sort.i2.why: Three out, which is about the limit of what losing is worth.
ch4.u4.sort.i3.label: Chlorine, 2,8,7
ch4.u4.sort.i3.why: One in and the shell is full. Far cheaper than losing seven.
ch4.u4.sort.i4.label: Oxygen, 2,6
ch4.u4.sort.i5.label: Neon, 2,8
ch4.u4.sort.i5.why: Already an octet. There is nothing to gain by changing.
ch4.u4.sort.i6.label: Argon, 2,8,8
ch4.u4.sort.i7.label: Carbon, 2,4
ch4.u4.sort.i7.why: Four out or four in are equally expensive, so carbon shares instead. That is why it builds chains rather than ions.
a.ch4-u4-sort-3.title: Lose, gain or neither?
a.ch4-u4-sort-3.blurb: Look at the outermost shell and decide which way the atom will go.
ch4.u4.quiz.q0.prompt: How many valence electrons does a chloride ion, Cl-, have?
ch4.u4.quiz.q0.f0: That is not a count of the outermost shell.
ch4.u4.quiz.q0.f1: Right. Chlorine has 7 and the ion has gained one, giving a full outer shell of 8.
ch4.u4.quiz.q0.f2: 17 is chlorine's atomic number, which counts protons, not valence electrons.
ch4.u4.quiz.q0.f3: 18 is the total number of electrons in the ion, not the number in the outer shell.
ch4.u4.quiz.q1.prompt: Why are the noble gases almost completely unreactive?
ch4.u4.quiz.q1.o0: Their atoms are too heavy to move
ch4.u4.quiz.q1.f0: Helium is one of the lightest atoms there is.
ch4.u4.quiz.q1.o1: Their outermost shells are already full
ch4.u4.quiz.q1.f1: Right. With a full outer shell there is nothing to gain by reacting.
ch4.u4.quiz.q1.f2: They have plenty. The point is how they are arranged.
ch4.u4.quiz.q1.o3: They are gases, and gases do not react
ch4.u4.quiz.q1.f3: Oxygen and hydrogen are gases and react readily.
a.ch4-u4-quiz-4.title: Valency from the shells
ch4.u5.definition: The atomic number Z is the number of protons, and it is what defines the element: change it and you have a different element entirely. The mass number A is the number of protons plus neutrons, which are together called nucleons, because the electrons weigh too little to count. An atom is written with A above and Z below its symbol.
a.ch4-u5-read-1.title: Two numbers: Z and A
ask.ch4-u5-zoom-2.empty.q: If the nucleus is that small, what is the rest of the atom?
ask.ch4-u5-zoom-2.empty.a:
Empty, in the only sense the word can have here.

The nucleus is about a hundred thousand times smaller across than the atom. Put the nucleus at the centre circle of a football pitch and the nearest electron is somewhere in the stands. Everything between is occupied by nothing but the electron's presence, which is not a thing sitting at a place.

That is what Rutherford's alpha particles were reporting. They mostly met nothing because there is mostly nothing to meet, and solid matter feeling solid is about electrical repulsion rather than about anything being full.
a.ch4-u5-zoom-2.title: The nucleus, on the same scale
a.ch4-u5-zoom-2.blurb: The bottom of the scale you have been climbing since the first chapter.
ch4.u5.calc.c0.prompt: An atom has atomic number 9 and 10 neutrons. What is its mass number?
ch4.u5.calc.c0.g0: Atomic number Z is 9, so 9 protons
ch4.u5.calc.c0.s0: Mass number is protons plus neutrons
ch4.u5.calc.c0.trap: Answering 10 by giving the neutrons alone, or 9 by giving the protons alone. A is both together.
ch4.u5.calc.c1.prompt: Sulphur has mass number 32 and atomic number 16. How many neutrons does it have?
ch4.u5.calc.c1.g1: Atomic number Z is 16, so 16 protons
ch4.u5.calc.c1.s0: Neutrons are the nucleons that are not protons
ch4.u5.calc.c1.trap: Adding instead of subtracting. A already includes the protons.
ch4.u5.calc.c2.prompt: An atom has mass number 24 and 12 protons. It is neutral. How many electrons does it have?
ch4.u5.calc.c2.s0: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons
ch4.u5.calc.c2.trap: Reaching for the mass number. The 24 tells you about the nucleus and says nothing about electrons.
a.ch4-u5-calc-3.title: Fill in the missing number
a.ch4-u5-calc-3.blurb: Protons, neutrons, electrons, Z and A. Any two of them give you the rest.
ch4.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: What decides which element an atom is?
ch4.u5.quiz.q0.f0: Change the neutrons and you have an isotope of the same element.
ch4.u5.quiz.q0.f1: Right. Elements are defined by their proton count, and nothing else.
ch4.u5.quiz.q0.f2: An ion has lost or gained electrons and is still the same element.
ch4.u5.quiz.q0.f3: Calcium and argon can share a mass number while being different elements.
ch4.u5.quiz.q1.prompt: Why is the mass of the electrons left out when working out mass number?
ch4.u5.quiz.q1.f0: True, but being outside is not why they are ignored. It is how little they weigh.
ch4.u5.quiz.q1.o1: An electron weighs about one two-thousandth of a proton, which rounds to nothing
ch4.u5.quiz.q1.f1: Right. Even in a heavy atom the electrons together are a fraction of one unit.
ch4.u5.quiz.q1.o2: Electrons have no mass at all
ch4.u5.quiz.q1.f2: They have a mass. It is tiny, not zero.
ch4.u5.quiz.q1.o3: The positive and negative masses cancel
ch4.u5.quiz.q1.f3: Mass does not come in positive and negative.
a.ch4-u5-quiz-4.title: Reading the two numbers
ch4.u6.definition: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, so the same atomic number and different mass numbers. Hydrogen has three: protium, deuterium and tritium. Because chemistry is decided by electrons, isotopes of an element behave identically in reactions and differ only in mass.
a.ch4-u6-read-1.title: Same element, different weight
ask.ch4-u6-tree-2.whysame.q: If isotopes have different masses, why do they behave the same chemically?
ask.ch4-u6-tree-2.whysame.a:
Because chemistry is electrons, and isotopes have identical electrons.

A reaction is outer-shell electrons being lost, gained or shared. The number of those is set by the proton count, which is identical across isotopes by definition. The extra neutrons sit in the nucleus adding mass and taking no part.

It is why you cannot separate isotopes by any chemical method, and why separating them needs something that notices mass directly, like a centrifuge. It is also why an isotope used as a medical tracer behaves in the body exactly like the ordinary version while being detectable.
a.ch4-u6-tree-2.title: Isotopes, isobars or neither?
a.ch4-u6-tree-2.blurb: Two atoms at a time. Two questions settle every pair.
ch4.u6.calc.c0.prompt: Chlorine occurs as chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 in the ratio 3 to 1. What is its average atomic mass?
ch4.u6.calc.c0.s0: Take 35 for three quarters of the atoms: 35 times 75 over 100
ch4.u6.calc.c0.s1: Take 37 for one quarter: 37 times 25 over 100
ch4.u6.calc.c0.trap: Averaging 35 and 37 to get 36. That would be right only if the two were equally common, and they are not.
ch4.u6.calc.c1.prompt: Bromine occurs as bromine-79 and bromine-81 in almost equal amounts, 49.7 percent and 50.3 percent. What is its average atomic mass, to the nearest whole number?
ch4.u6.calc.c1.s0: The two are so nearly equal that the average sits almost exactly between them
ch4.u6.calc.c1.trap: Assuming it must land on one of the two masses. An average rarely equals any single member.
a.ch4-u6-calc-3.title: Averaging the isotopes
a.ch4-u6-calc-3.blurb: An element's atomic mass is the average of its isotopes, weighted by how common each one is.
ch4.u6.quiz.q0.prompt: Isotopes of an element have what in common, and what differs?
ch4.u6.quiz.q0.o0: Same number of neutrons, different protons
ch4.u6.quiz.q0.f0: That is the wrong way round, and it describes nothing that exists.
ch4.u6.quiz.q0.o1: Same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons
ch4.u6.quiz.q0.f1: Right. Same Z, different A, same element.
ch4.u6.quiz.q0.o2: Same mass number, different atomic number
ch4.u6.quiz.q0.f3: Isotopes share their chemistry exactly, because they share their electrons.
ch4.u6.quiz.q1.prompt: Calcium-40 and argon-40 have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. What are they?
ch4.u6.quiz.q1.f0: Isotopes share the atomic number. These do not.
ch4.u6.quiz.q1.f1: Right. Same A, different Z, so different elements entirely.
ch4.u6.quiz.q1.f2: Different proton counts mean different elements.
ch4.u6.quiz.q1.f3: Perfectly possible, and it is what isobar means.
a.ch4-u6-quiz-4.title: Telling them apart
mis.electron-is-heavy.statement: An electron weighs about as much as a proton.
mis.electron-is-heavy.correction: It is roughly one two-thousandth of a proton, which is why mass number ignores electrons entirely.
mis.neutron-is-the-light-one.statement: The neutron is the lightest of the three particles.
mis.neutron-is-the-light-one.correction: It is one of the two heavy ones, near enough the same mass as a proton. The electron is the light one.
mis.atom-has-no-charges.statement: A neutral atom contains no charged particles.
mis.atom-has-no-charges.correction: It contains plenty of both kinds. Neutral means they are equal in number, not absent.
mis.neutrons-cancel-charge.statement: Neutrons balance the charge of the protons.
mis.neutrons-cancel-charge.correction: Neutrons have no charge, so they cancel nothing. The electrons balance the protons.
mis.charge-leaks-away.statement: An atom is neutral because any extra charge leaks away.
mis.charge-leaks-away.correction: Nothing leaks. The proton and electron counts are equal to begin with.
mis.scattering-found-electron.statement: The gold foil experiment discovered the electron.
mis.scattering-found-electron.correction: Thomson found the electron before it, by other means. Scattering found the nucleus.
mis.scattering-found-proton.statement: The gold foil experiment discovered the proton.
mis.scattering-found-proton.correction: It showed a dense positive centre existed. The proton came from Goldstein's canal rays.
mis.scattering-found-neutron.statement: The gold foil experiment discovered the neutron.
mis.scattering-found-neutron.correction: Chadwick found the neutron in 1932, decades later and by a different route.
mis.foil-has-holes.statement: Alpha particles passed through because the foil had holes in it.
mis.foil-has-holes.correction: The foil was continuous. The empty space is inside each atom, not between them.
mis.alpha-is-small.statement: Alpha particles passed through because they are small.
mis.alpha-is-small.correction: They are large and heavy as particles go. They passed through because there was nothing in the way.
mis.gold-is-soft.statement: Gold was chosen because it is soft.
mis.gold-is-soft.correction: Gold was chosen because it can be beaten thinner than any other metal, and thinness is what makes a single rebound meaningful.
mis.shells-fill-outside-in.statement: Electrons fill the outer shells first.
mis.shells-fill-outside-in.correction: They fill from the nucleus outwards. A shell does not begin until the ones inside it are full.
mis.shells-fill-out-of-order.statement: Shells can be filled in any order.
mis.shells-fill-out-of-order.correction: They fill strictly inside out, which is what makes an electron distribution predictable.
mis.forgets-inner-shell.statement: Only the outermost shell counts towards the total.
mis.forgets-inner-shell.correction: Every electron counts towards the total. Only the outermost ones count towards chemistry.
mis.forgets-outer-shell.statement: A full K shell is the whole of a small atom.
mis.forgets-outer-shell.correction: K holds only 2. Anything past helium has started on L.
mis.counts-unfilled-shell.statement: An electron total includes shells that have not been filled.
mis.counts-unfilled-shell.correction: An empty shell holds nothing. Count what is actually there.
mis.miscounts-valence.statement: Valence electrons are counted across all shells.
mis.miscounts-valence.correction: Only the outermost shell. The inner electrons take no part in reactions.
mis.confuses-z-with-valence.statement: The atomic number is the valency.
mis.confuses-z-with-valence.correction: Atomic number counts protons. Valency counts how many electrons the outer shell must move.
mis.counts-all-electrons.statement: Valence electrons means the total number of electrons.
mis.counts-all-electrons.correction: It means the ones in the outermost shell, which is usually a much smaller number.
mis.heavy-means-unreactive.correction: Helium is among the lightest atoms and among the least reactive. Reactivity is about the outer shell.
mis.noble-gas-has-no-electrons.statement: Noble gases are unreactive because they have no electrons.
mis.noble-gas-has-no-electrons.correctio: They have a full complement. It is the fullness of the outer shell that makes them unreactive.
mis.gases-do-not-react.statement: Gases do not take part in reactions.
mis.gases-do-not-react.correction: Hydrogen and oxygen are gases and react vigorously. The state has nothing to do with it.
mis.neutrons-define-element.statement: The number of neutrons decides which element an atom is.
mis.neutrons-define-element.correction: The proton count decides it. Change the neutrons and you have an isotope of the same element.
mis.electrons-define-element.statement: The number of electrons decides which element an atom is.
mis.electrons-define-element.correction: An ion has gained or lost electrons and is still the same element.
mis.mass-number-defines-element.statemen: The mass number decides which element an atom is.
mis.mass-number-defines-element.correcti: Calcium-40 and argon-40 share a mass number and are different elements.
mis.electrons-excluded-by-position.state: Electrons are left out of mass number because they sit outside the nucleus.
mis.electrons-excluded-by-position.corre: They are left out because they weigh almost nothing. Mass number counts nucleons, and that is a definition rather than an oversight.
mis.electron-has-no-mass.correction: It has a small one. Small enough to ignore in sums, not zero.
mis.mass-cancels.statement: Positive and negative masses cancel out.
mis.mass-cancels.correction: Mass has no sign. Only charge does.
mis.isotope-differs-in-protons.statement: Isotopes differ in their number of protons.
mis.isotope-differs-in-protons.correctio: They share their protons exactly. It is the neutrons that differ.
mis.isotope-confused-with-isobar.stateme: Isotopes have the same mass number.
mis.isotope-confused-with-isobar.correct: Isobars have the same mass number. Isotopes have the same atomic number.
mis.isotopes-differ-chemically.statement: Isotopes of an element react differently.
mis.isotopes-differ-chemically.correctio: They react identically, because chemistry is decided by electrons and isotopes have the same ones.
mis.same-mass-same-element.statement: Two atoms with the same mass number are the same element.
mis.same-mass-same-element.correction: Calcium-40 and argon-40 are the counterexample.
mis.isobars-impossible.statement: Two different elements cannot share a mass number.
mis.isobars-impossible.correction: They can, and when they do they are called isobars.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: Rubbing a comb on your hair makes it pick up paper. What does that tell you about what matter is made of?
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: That ordinary matter contains charged pieces that can be moved. Nothing was created by the rubbing, so the charge was already there, inside both the hair and the comb.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'the comb became magnetic'. Magnetism and static charge feel similar at this scale and are not the same thing, and the confusion survives all the way to Class 10 if nobody names it.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: An atom is electrically neutral. Does that mean it contains no charged particles?
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: No. It contains equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the charges cancel. Neutral means balanced, not empty.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'it has no charge in it'. It is a reasonable reading of the word and it is exactly backwards.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: Most alpha particles went straight through the gold foil. What did Rutherford conclude from that alone?
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: That most of the atom is empty space. There was simply nothing in the way for most of them.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'the foil had holes'. It is continuous foil; the emptiness is inside the atoms rather than between them.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: Thomson's model explained one thing well. What was it, and what killed the model?
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: It explained why atoms are neutral, with positive and negative in equal measure. It died because a thinly spread positive charge cannot turn a fast alpha particle around, and about one in twelve thousand came back.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for an answer that says the model was simply wrong. It was right about neutrality and wrong about the arrangement, and that distinction is how science usually moves.
recap.s.u2.q3.ask: Why could Rutherford's atom not be stable?
recap.s.u2.q3.answer: An electron going round a circle is accelerating, and accelerating charges radiate energy. It would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus almost at once.
recap.s.u2.q3.listenFor: Listen for 'the electron would fly off'. The problem is the opposite: it falls in.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: How many electrons fit in the M shell, and how many are allowed in it when it is the outermost shell?
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: The capacity is 2n squared, so 18. But no outermost shell may hold more than 8, so an atom that ends at M stops at 8 and starts the N shell.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for a flat 18 with no mention of the outermost rule. It is the rule that explains why potassium starts a fourth shell rather than putting a ninth electron in M.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: Sodium has 11 electrons. How are they arranged in its shells?
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: 2,8,1. K takes 2, L takes 8, and the eleventh goes into M.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for 2,9 or 8,2,1. The first ignores the capacity of L, the second fills from the outside in.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Magnesium is 2,8,2 and chlorine is 2,8,7. Why does magnesium have a valency of two and chlorine one?
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: Magnesium has two electrons in its outer shell and loses both. Chlorine has seven and needs only one more to fill its shell, so it gains one.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'chlorine has seven, so its valency is seven'. Losing seven is far harder than gaining one, and the atom always takes the shorter route.
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: Its outermost shell already holds eight electrons. There is nothing to gain by losing, gaining or sharing, so it does not react.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because it is a gas'. Oxygen and hydrogen are gases and react readily.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: An atom has atomic number 16 and mass number 32. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does it have?
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: 16 protons, because that is the atomic number. 16 neutrons, because 32 minus 16. And 16 electrons, because a neutral atom matches its protons.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for 32 neutrons. The mass number already includes the protons, so the neutrons are what is left after subtracting them.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: Why is the mass of an atom worked out from protons and neutrons only?
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: Because an electron weighs about one two-thousandth of a proton. Even in a heavy atom all the electrons together come to a fraction of one unit.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'electrons have no mass'. They have a small one, and small is not zero.
recap.s.u6.q1.ask: Chlorine's atomic mass is 35.5 u. Which chlorine atom weighs 35.5 u?
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: None of them. Every chlorine atom is either 35 or 37. The 35.5 is an average weighted by how common each is, three to one, and it belongs to the element rather than to any atom.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Listen for a student who takes 35.5 as a real atom with half a nucleon in it. Nucleons do not come in halves, and noticing that is what makes the average idea necessary.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: Calcium-40 and argon-40. Isotopes or isobars, and how do you know?
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: Isobars. They share a mass number of 40 and have different atomic numbers, 20 and 18, so they are different elements.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: Listen for isotopes. The two words sound alike and the distinction is the whole of this topic: isotopes share the atomic number, isobars share the mass number.
aid.s.u6.meaning: Five tests, and one word for both. Run down the list for isotopes and everything matches except the last. Run down it for isobars and nothing matches except the last. M is the odd one out both times, which is the whole distinction.

gloss.electron: A negatively charged particle outside the nucleus, with about one two-thousandth of the mass of a proton.
gloss.proton: A positively charged particle in the nucleus. How many there are decides which element the atom is.
gloss.neutron: A particle in the nucleus with no charge and about the same mass as a proton.
gloss.nucleus: The tiny dense centre of an atom, holding the protons and neutrons and nearly all of its mass.
gloss.nucleon: A proton or a neutron. The mass number counts them together.
gloss.shell: One of the fixed levels an electron may occupy, counted outwards from the nucleus and named K, L, M, N. A shell numbered n holds at most 2n squared electrons.
gloss.valence-electron: An electron in the outermost shell. These are the only ones that take part in chemical reactions.
gloss.octet: A full outermost shell of eight electrons, which is stable and unreactive. Atoms lose, gain or share electrons to reach one.
gloss.valency: How many electrons an atom must lose, gain or share to reach a full outer shell. It is the combining capacity Chapter 3 called an arm.
gloss.atomic-number: The number of protons in an atom, written Z. It defines the element.
gloss.mass-number: The number of protons plus neutrons, written A. Electrons are too light to count.
gloss.isotope: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons: same atomic number, different mass numbers. They are chemically identical.
gloss.isobar: Atoms of different elements that happen to share a mass number, such as calcium-40 and argon-40.
gloss.alpha-particle: A doubly charged helium ion, mass 4 u. Rutherford fired them at gold foil and discovered the nucleus.
